hints: Transform the endpoints: $x=0$ and $x=1$ give the corresponding values of $\theta$.
Cancel the powers of $\sec\theta$ to obtain the stated $\cos^2\theta$ integral.
walkthrough:
Differentiate the substitution $x = \sqrt{3}\tan\theta$ with respect to $\theta$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \sqrt{3}\sec^2\theta \implies \mathrm{d}x = \sqrt{3}\sec^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Convert the limits of integration from $x$ to $\theta$:
When $x = 0$:
$$0 = \sqrt{3}\tan\theta \implies \tan\theta = 0 \implies \theta = 0$$
When $x = 1$:
$$1 = \sqrt{3}\tan\theta \implies \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

Express the denominator $(3 + x^2)^2$ in terms of $\theta$ using the identity $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$:
$$3 + x^2 = 3 + (\sqrt{3}\tan\theta)^2 = 3 + 3\tan^2\theta = 3(1 + \tan^2\theta) = 3\sec^2\theta$$
$$(3 + x^2)^2 = (3\sec^2\theta)^2 = 9\sec^4\theta$$

Substitute $x$, $(3 + x^2)^2$, and $\mathrm{d}x$ into the integral $I$:
$$I = \int_0^{\pi/6} \dfrac{9}{9\sec^4\theta} \cdot \left(\sqrt{3}\sec^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\right) = \sqrt{3}\int_0^{\pi/6} \dfrac{\sec^2\theta}{\sec^4\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \sqrt{3}\int_0^{\pi/6} \dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Use the reciprocal identity $\dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta} = \cos^2\theta$ to obtain the required expression:
$$I = \sqrt{3}\int_0^{\pi/6} \cos^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

ai_rubric.Integration by Substitution: Identifies $dx=\sqrt3\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$; Substitutes for $x$ and $dx$ throughout; Concludes with $I=\sqrt3\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$.

hints: Integrate to $\tfrac12\theta+\tfrac14\sin2\theta$ and apply the bounds $0$ and $\pi/6$.
Multiply by $\sqrt3$ and simplify the exact terms.
walkthrough:
Apply the double angle formula $\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1$ to rewrite the integrand $\cos^2\theta$:
$$\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2\theta$$

Substitute this into the expression for $I$:
$$I = \sqrt{3}\int_0^{\pi/6} \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2\theta\right)\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin\left(2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{12} + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{12} + \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{12} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{8}$$

Evaluate the antiderivative at the lower limit $\theta = 0$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}(0) + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin(0) = 0$$

Multiply the evaluated definite integral by $\sqrt{3}$:
$$I = \sqrt{3}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{8}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{12} + \dfrac{(\sqrt{3})(\sqrt{3})}{8} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{12} + \dfrac{3}{8}$$

ai_rubric.Integration: Rewrites integrand by $\frac12\cos2\theta+\frac12$. Substitutes limits in an integral of the form $c\sin2\theta+b\theta$, where $cb\ne0$. Concludes with $I=\frac{\sqrt3\pi}{12}+\frac38$.
